\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{بدعنوانی} (badunvānī)}{بدعنوانی (badunvānī)}]{\ur{بدعنوانی} (badunvānī) — corruption}

\label{lesson:UR-C357-badunvani}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to put right, then the Urdu for to polish a skill.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{بدعنوانی}}
\textbf{\ur{بدعنوانی}} — \emph{badunvānī} — \textquotedblleft{}corruption\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{حکومت} \ur{بدعنوانی} \ur{کے} \ur{خلاف} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{hukūmat badunvānī ke khilāf hai.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The government is against corruption.
\end{quote}

Feminine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{بدعنوانی}} (\emph{badunvānī}) is built from Persian \emph{bad}, \textquotedblleft{}bad\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{unvān}, \textquotedblleft{}a heading; a manner\textquotedblright{}, which is usually traced, through Persian, to Arabic \emph{ʿunwān}, with the noun ending \emph{-ī}. Urdu uses it for corruption, bad conduct in office, a sense our sources do not trace.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for giving reasons and opinions.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{badunvānī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{badunvānī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{hukūmat badunvānī ke khilāf hai.} — The government is against corruption.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for to put right, then the Urdu for to polish a skill, then say \emph{badunvānī} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ur{بدعنوانی} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Corruption\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
